transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-04-08 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Brightlane Eng), Tom Baker (Brightlane CTO), Olivia Park (Brightlane PM)

Summary (auto): Intro to Redwood hosted generation API. Demo covers streaming options, parameter effects, retry/backoff behavior, and proposed pilot.

[00:00] Ava (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ava, I'll be the AE on this. We also have Liam from engineering. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya: Good, thanks. Excited to see the onramp.
[00:12] Ava: Great. Quick agenda: we'll walk through the hosted gen endpoints, show live streaming with a sample chat, discuss tuning parameters—temp, top_p, max tokens, stop sequences—then Liam will run through retries and backoff patterns. We'll finish with next steps for a pilot. Sound OK?
[00:29] Tom: Yep, sounds good. We care a lot about tail latency and not replaying half-baked partial outputs to users.
[00:36] Liam (Redwood SE): Totally understood. We'll demo how streaming chunks arrive and best practices for safe rehydration, plus idempotency for retries.
[00:45] Olivia: Quick question before we start: are you showing server-sent events or websockets?
[00:50] Ava: We'll demo SSE first—it's our default streaming mode for the REST endpoint—then show websocket flow for lower-latency two-way streams.

--- Live demo portion starts ---

[01:10] Liam: Ok switching to the sandbox. I'm calling the /generate.chat endpoint with a small conversation. Temperature set to 0.2, max_tokens 120, top_p 0.95. You can see the stream of deltas coming in.
[01:28] (sound of typing, faint background)
[01:33] Maya: I see partial tokens arriving, is there a char buffer you recommend at the client to avoid mid-word flashes?
[01:40] Liam: Yeah, we commonly suggest a 150ms debounce or accumulate until whitespace punctuation, basically heuristics to avoid flashing mid-token. There's also a chunk_mode param—if you set chunk_mode: sentence you'll get sentence-level emits when possible. Note: chunking can add a few ms of latency.
[02:05] Tom: And what about reconnects? If the stream drops mid-response what happens server-side?
[02:12] Liam: By default, a streaming session has a short-lived server buffer; we don't keep an open KV of partial responses indefinitely. For safety we recommend the client maintain the conversation state and on reconnect re-issue the request with a resume_token if you want server continuation. Resume is optional; otherwise a retry will trigger a regenerated response from the last accepted user message. Resume_token is ephemeral — TTL of ~30s.
[02:40] Maya: Hmm 30s might be tight for mobile networks. Could we extend that?
[02:44] Liam: For Dedicated or Private customers we can extend the TTL or enable sticky routing, yes. On Hosted we keep conservative TTLs for resource fairness.

[03:01] Ava: Quick note on params: lower temperature reduces variance, top_p trims tail probability mass, and repetition_penalty helps with hallucinations on long prompts. We showed temp 0.2; for more creative outputs you bump to 0.8.
[03:18] Olivia: Does Redwood enforce token limits? We have to ensure no runaway bills.
[03:22] Ava: Yes, we have per-request max_tokens and also per-account hard caps. You can enable guardrails in the Console to reject requests exceeding thresholds. We'll include console screenshots in the follow-up.

[03:40] Liam: Now for retries—common pattern is client-driven exponential backoff with jitter. Example: initial retry after 300ms, then 900ms, 2.7s, etc. Always check for idempotency_token per request; if the server receives the same idempotency token the request can be treated as safe to retry without double-charging tokens for completed generations.
[04:02] Tom: So idempotency applies to sync calls only or streaming too?
[04:06] Liam: You can attach idempotency_token to streaming sessions as well. If the request completes server-side, replays with the same token will return the cached output. For partially completed streams the behavior is: if we have a cached final response, we re-emit it; otherwise the server treats it as a new run but if a resume_token is provided we attempt continuation. There are edge cases, we documented them in the runbook.

[04:30] Maya: I'm worried about partial replays — user sees partial, then after reconnect a fully different completion appears. How do you recommend UX handles that?
[04:38] Liam: Two approaches: optimistic streaming where you show partial, but mark as tentative until final delta arrives; or client-side buffering where you don't display until final chunk. For chat UIs we see a hybrid—show partial with a loading indicator, and if final differs significantly you fade-in the correction. There's also a compare endpoint we can call to diff candidates.

[05:05] Olivia: Can you demo a retry scenario live?
[05:09] Liam: Sure — I'll intentionally drop the stream. (pause) Dropped. Now I resend with idempotency token x-123, backoff starts, and after the second attempt we get the cached final result. See the UI popped the same content.
[05:30] Maya: Nice. Is there any per-request billing anomaly if we retry multiple times?
[05:34] Ava: If the retry returns a cached final response we don't charge for a full generation again; only the first completed run counts. If the retry triggers a new generation you get billed for the new tokens. That's why idempotency + caching matters.

[06:00] Tom: What about concurrency and rate limits? We have bursts from product events—can we pin throughput?
[06:07] Ava: On Hosted we have quota controls and per-account rate limits; for predictable burst throughput the Dedicated offering is recommended where you reserve GPU pools. For Hosted you can request quota increases; we also have a burst token system for short spikes.

[06:30] Liam: Switching topics quickly — parameter tuning to control latency/cost: smaller model families and quantized variants give sublinear token costs and lower latency. Also enable prefix caching for repeated system prompts to cut down compute on long histories. We can suggest tuning per workload.

[07:00] Maya: Do you do automatic batching on Hosted? We care about latency but also want cost efficiency.
[07:05] Liam: Yes, runtime does continuous batching when it benefits throughput; we have policies to limit batch window to maintain latency SLOs. You can set a latency SLO per route in the Console and the runtime will adapt batching aggressiveness.

[07:30] Olivia: Security — do you persist logs or conversation data by default?
[07:34] Ava: By default, minimal telemetry is kept for X days for debugging. For customers that require no retention we offer data retention controls and Private deployment. We are SOC 2 Type II certified; we'll send the security pack. We also support customer-managed keys (KMS) and SSO via SAML.
[07:58] Tom: Can you provide audit log snippets? Our compliance team will want a sample.
[08:02] Ava: Yes, action item — we'll share an anonymized audit log and the SOC 2 artifact.

[08:20] Liam: Back to streaming: an operational note — when you set stop sequences, the model may still emit additional tokens if decoding probabilities cross thresholds. Stop sequences are best-effort. We recommend adding short explicit tokens and a finalizer check client-side.

[08:45] Maya: For our product flows we often need both short completions and longer summaries. Do you suggest separate routes?
[08:52] Liam: Yes, separate endpoints/routes with different model configs is a common pattern—low-latency small models for quick queries and larger models for summarize/batch jobs. Console routes let you pin models and ramp traffic with canary policies.

[09:15] Ava: I'll show the Console later but first a couple of failure-mode best practices: 1) set client-level timeouts to avoid orphaned waits, 2) show graceful fallback (canned message) if stream fails, 3) capture partials and attach to logs for triage.

[09:43] (screen share: Console)
[09:48] Ava: Here's the routes panel — you can set per-route SLOs, a standby fallback model and a canary rollout. For example route 'chat-default' has model: rwd-3b-quant, fallback: rwd-1b-quant, canary 5% for a new gen.
[10:10] Maya: Can we set cost thresholds that auto-fallback on budget exceed?
[10:15] Ava: Yes — in Optimize you can set cost per-token thresholds and a policy to fall back to cheaper variants automatically. We'll attach an example policy.

[10:35] Liam: Quick note on SDKs: our SDKs surface retries, streaming, and resume primitives. In JS we expose a stream.on('delta') and stream.on('final') hook. For reconnects we provide helper that will attempt resume with exponential backoff and surface a resume_token to the app.

[11:00] Tom: Any language-specific gotchas?
[11:03] Liam: In mobile apps watch the socket lifecycle — backgrounding can drop sockets and you need to re issue with resume. Also keep an eye on token counting with unicode grapheme clusters — our tokenization sometimes differs from naive char counts.

[11:28] Maya: Can you walk us through a minimal example of robust client code for streaming with retry?
[11:33] Liam: Sure, pseudo code: 1) issue request with idempotency_token and resume enabled; 2) on delta append to buffer and render as tentative; 3) on 'final' reconcile and mark stable; 4) on network error, trigger exponential backoff with jitter and retry using same idempotency token; 5) if retry hits a cached final response return it; 6) if not, re-issue with resume_token if available. We'll drop sample in the repo.

[12:05] (brief pause)
[12:10] Olivia: About pricing—are streaming tokens charged at the same rate?
[12:14] Ava: Yes tokens consumed by generation are billed; streaming itself has no additional charge. However partial retries that trigger regeneration will increase token counts. We'll include an estimator for expected monthly token consumption for your projected QPS.

[12:35] Maya: Our acceptance criteria for the pilot: median p50 latency < 220ms for 90% of queries, p95 < 600ms, and no more than 1 user-visible divergence on reconnection in test scenarios. Is that achievable?
[12:47] Liam: Likely yes for smaller models and with prefix caching enabled; for larger summarization flows p95 will be higher. We can scope the pilot to the most latency-sensitive endpoints.

[13:05] Tom: Do you support per-route rate limiting and SSO-based RBAC?
[13:10] Ava: Yes, per-route rate limits and SAML SSO with role mappings are supported. We'll include docs showing role->route mappings.

[13:30] Liam: Now a quick deep-dive on backoff parameters — recommended pattern: base=300ms, multiplier=3, max=8s, jitter=full. For example retry delays: 0.3s, 0.9s, 2.7s, 8s. Cap at 3 retries by default. We also recommend different retry budget for idempotent read-only style calls vs heavy long-generation calls.

[14:05] Maya: If a user gets charged because a retry triggered a new generation due to race, is there a way to dispute?
[14:11] Ava: We handle disputed charges on a case-by-case basis, but idempotency tokens plus observability reduces that significantly. We'll share the billing dispute process.

[14:30] (Liam shares benchmark chart)
[14:35] Liam: Here's some internal benchmarks—rwd-3b median latency at 128 tokens ~ 110ms, p95 ~ 420ms on our hosted fleet. These are sample numbers, your workload may vary. We can run a focused benchmark with your prompt set.

[15:00] Maya: Let's schedule that benchmark. We'll share prompt sets and traffic pattern.

[15:05] Ava: Great. A few more advanced controls: prefix caching, response deduplication, and token budgeting per user session. Those can be toggled in Console or via API configs.

[15:30] Olivia: Do you have a recommended retry policy for mobile clients specifically?
[15:34] Liam: Yes—mobile clients probably should use slightly longer base backoff (500ms) and lower retry cap because of battery and network churn. Also use resume_token rather than a blind retry to avoid duplicate long runs.

[16:00] Tom: Any mention of content safety? We need to sanitize outputs for user-facing content.
[16:05] Ava: We provide content filtering hooks and a moderation endpoint. You can run model output through our safety classifier before surfacing. We'll attach the moderation API doc.

[16:25] (brief side conversation, some crosstalk)
[16:40] Maya: Hypothetical—what if we want a hybrid: hosted for dev + dedicated for prod. How does rollout look?
[16:47] Ava: That's a common pattern. You can start on Hosted, pin model versions, then lift-and-shift to Dedicated. We support export of model configs and the same API surface so code changes are minimal. Runtime orchestration handles the rest.

[17:10] Liam: For the pilot we'll propose three routes: placeholder-chat (low latency), story-summarize (higher quality, bigger model), and fallback. We'll recommend canary 10% then ramp.

[17:30] Maya: Anything else on observability during the pilot?
[17:33] Ava: We'll enable per-token costs, latency percentiles, and trace sampling. You can pull logs into your SIEM via our audit streaming.

[17:50] (questions from Olivia on rollout timing)
[18:02] Olivia: If pilot is 2 weeks how quickly can you provision Dedicated if we need it?
[18:07] Ava: Dedicated lead time varies—usually 2–6 weeks depending on GPU inventory and region. We'll keep Hosted as a fallback.

[18:25] (short pause)
[18:40] Liam: One more note — when tuning stop sequences and max_tokens, the model can still exceed stop heuristics if sampling crosses. So always have a post-process sanitizer. Also for streaming you can set a soft_stop flag to do a last-token check before emitting final delta.

[19:10] Tom: That's helpful. Okay let's recap and confirm next steps.

[19:20] Ava: Recap: 1) Redwood to send pilot pricing + security pack; 2) SE to share benchmark harness and sample client code for streaming+retry; 3) Brightlane to share prompt sets and acceptance criteria; 4) schedule pilot kickoff week of 2027-04-18.
[19:40] Maya: We'll get prompts over by Tuesday.
[19:42] Ava: Perfect. Any last questions?
[19:46] Tom: Nothing on my end. Thanks.
[19:49] Olivia: No, good session.
[19:52] (call ends, small chatter)

Notes on transcription: some proper nouns may be off; occasional speaker label mismatches (Speaker 7 was uncertain). Links shared: https://redwood.ai/docs/streams (demo console), https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (security pack).

End of transcript.
